title: False king, false subjects
hookLine: false the king, false the subjects, false the whole world, and still we love it (Asa di Var, ang 468)

lines: A PALACE WITH A GIFT SHOP.
A SALOK THAT STARTS WITH THE KING.
cards: Old cities are full of the leftovers of someone's empire. A gate that once had guards. A palace that is now a museum, with a gift shop where the throne room used to be.

Whoever built it surely meant it to stand forever. In Guru Nanak's lifetime, Punjab watched one ruling house fall and another rise: the Lodi sultans gave way to Babur and the Mughals. He saw power change hands up close.
And in the Asa di Var there's a salok that starts with the king himself and works down to everything we own and love.

teach.b: The word that repeats is koorh, and it runs through the salok on ang 468, phrase after phrase. In paraphrase: koorh is the king, koorh the subjects, koorh the whole world.

Koorh are the mansions and palaces, and koorh the ones who live in them. Koorh is gold, koorh is silver, koorh are those who wear them. Koorh is the body, koorh the clothes, koorh the matchless beauty.
Koorh is the husband, koorh the wife; they waste away and are gone. Koorh usually gets translated false. But here it means something gentler and sadder than lying.
It means what passes. What looks solid and isn't.
Gold is real gold, a palace is a real palace, a marriage is a real marriage, but none of them can hold you up forever. Then the turn: and still we love it.
The false, the salok says, fall in love with the false and forget the Creator. With whom should we make friends? The whole world is passing away.
Falsehood is sweet, falsehood is honey; falsehood drowns boatloads of people.
And the salok ends with Nanak's plea to the One: without you, everything is koorh, koorh. Sikh teachers are careful here.
Guru Nanak, as Sikhs remember him, was a householder who married, raised a family, and in his later years farmed at Kartarpur. Sikhs aren't asked to leave the world or despise it.
The point is where the heart leans its full weight.

teach.h: LIVE IN IT; DON'T LEAN ON IT.
teach.b: Love your people, use the silver, live in the house.
Just don't mistake any of it for the thing that lasts.

how: Sikhs hear this salok of koorh in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and Sikh teaching holds that a householder lives fully in the world while knowing that all of it passes.

o: what passes, though it looks solid
an impostor on a stolen throne
a ruler who tells outright lies

games.q: koorh, the passing — tap the pairs.

s: in this salok, koorh only means telling lies
it means what passes, what looks solid and isn't.
Sikhs are asked to leave the world because it is koorh
Guru Nanak was a householder; the point is where the heart leans its full weight.
the salok calls falsehood sweet, like honey
and says it drowns boatloads of people.

games.q: the whole world, the salok says, is passing away. what does Guru Nanak ask?
o: with whom should we make friends?
how can we build something that lasts forever?
why should we bother at all?
games.why: with whom should we make friends? the whole world is passing away. the salok ends: without you, all is koorh.

practice: Let your eyes rest on one thing you care about, a mug, a photograph, a ring, and look at it as if this were your last week with it.
Notice the tenderness and the grip, then breathe out and loosen the grip a little, without letting go of the care. If you pray, say Waheguru, the One who doesn't pass.

wordCard.voice: False king. Koorh, the false, the passing: king, subjects, palaces, gold and beauty. Without the One, Guru Nanak says, all of it is koorh.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: koorh, the false, the unreal, what passes; the opposite of sach, truth.

carryVoice: Your line: it won't last. The care can stay; the grip can loosen. Five hundred forty-eight days.

sources.ref: Asa di Var, salok M1 (koorh raajaa koorh parjaa), Ang 468
